  over every file and opens the upload modal.

3:A desktop application for post-processing PDF files containing batches of scanned documents. The app has three modes: **Merge**, **Split**, and **Drive Upload**.
4-
5-## Tech stack
6-
7-- **Desktop framework**: Wails
8-- **Backend**: Go
9-- **Frontend**: TypeScript + React
10-- **UI components**: Mantine
11-- **Virtualization**: TanStack Virtual
12-- **Drag-and-drop**: dnd-kit
13-- **PDF manipulation**: pdfcpu
14-- **PDF rendering** (thumbnails): `pdftoppm` (Poppler, system install, called as subprocess)
15-
16-## Common elements
17-
18-Both modes include a thumbnail panel and a page detail panel, and support the same per-page editing operations.
19-
20-### Thumbnail panel
21-
22-A vertically scrolling strip of page thumbnails. Width is user-adjustable via a drag handle; thumbnails scale to fill the panel width. Rendering is on-demand and virtualized — only visible thumbnails (plus a small overscan buffer) are rendered at any given time.
23-
24-The Go backend exposes a per-page render method returning a base64-encoded PNG; the frontend requests thumbnails as they scroll into view (`pdftoppm` subprocess).
25-
26-#### Keyboard shortcuts
27-
28-| Key                    | Action                                     |
29-| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
30-| `R`                    | Rotate selected page clockwise 90°         |
31-| `Shift+R`              | Rotate selected page counter-clockwise 90° |
32-| `Delete` / `Backspace` | Toggle skip on the selected page           |
33-| `←` / `→`              | Select previous / next page                |
34-
35-### Page detail panel
36-
37-Shows the currently selected page at reading resolution. Selecting a thumbnail updates it.
38-
39-Supports:
40-
41-- **Pan**: drag to pan.
42-- **Zoom**: scroll wheel or trackpad pinch to zoom in/out.
43-- **Navigate**: `←` / `→` to move to the previous/next page.
44-
45-Implemented with `react-zoom-pan-pinch`.
46-
47-### Page editing
48-
49-Individual pages can be edited in both modes before export or merge:
50-
51-- **Rotation**: pages can be rotated in 90° increments (clockwise or counter-clockwise).
52-- **Skip**: pages can be marked as skipped — excluded from the output but remaining visible in the thumbnail view (greyed out). A page is skipped by clicking a skip icon that appears on hover, or via keyboard shortcut.
53-- **Reorder**: pages can be reordered by dragging thumbnails to a new position.
54-
55-## Mode: Merge
56-
57-For scanners that can only scan one side at a time. The user scans all front pages as one PDF and all back pages as another, then uses Merge mode to interleave them into a single PDF.
58-
59-### Workflow
60-
61-1. The user loads two PDF files, labelled **File A** and **File B**.
62-2. The user selects which file contains the first page (**First page in: File A / File B**).
63-3. A **Reverse File B** checkbox controls whether File B is reversed before interleaving. This should be checked when the paper stack was flipped between scans (the typical case, when scanning one side at a time), causing the second-scanned pages to be in reverse order.
64-4. The app interleaves the pages: A1, B1, A2, B2, etc.
65-5. The user saves the merged result as a new PDF file on disk.
66-
67-The merged PDF can then be opened in Split mode for further processing.
68-
69-### Unequal page counts
70-
71-If File A and File B have different page counts, the app shows a warning before proceeding: "File A has X pages, File B has Y pages. The extra Z page(s) will be appended at the end." The user can cancel or continue. The extra pages from the longer file are appended in order after the interleaved section.
72-

Before writing feature code, if there's cleanup to do (unused props, dead code, a component that should move to a shared location, etc.), point it out and ask whether to clean up first. This is about commit *sequencing* with this user, not a rule about resulting repo content, so it lives in memory rather than CLAUDE.md — see [[feedback_memory_vs_claudemd]].

**How to apply:** When starting a feature, scan the files to be modified for unused/dead code or things that should move/get extracted. If found, mention it before writing any feature code. metadata:

Never run `git commit` unless the user has explicitly asked for it in this turn. An earlier "commit" instruction does not authorize committing again later in the session — each commit (or batch of commits for one piece of work) needs its own explicit go-ahead. After finishing a reviewable chunk of work, stop and ask whether to commit; don't just do it because that's the rhythm the conversation fell into.

**Why:** User corrected this on 2026-07-02: after saying "commit" once (for Step 2 work), I kept committing on my own for subsequent steps (Step 3a, a test-infra fix, Step 3b) without being asked again each time. This is about the approval relationship with this specific user — a different user of this repo might not want that friction at all — so it belongs in memory, not CLAUDE.md. See [[feedback_memory_vs_claudemd]].

**How to apply:** Finish the work, run verification (build/test/typecheck), summarize what changed, and explicitly ask "want me to commit this?" — then wait. Do not commit proactively even if the previous turn's work was committed after a similar request. This applies within a single session and especially across multiple pieces of work in a row (e.g. a multi-step checklist implementation) — each step's commit needs its own confirmation, not just the first one. See also [[feedback_separate_commits]] for how to split what does get committed once confirmed.

**Show the commit message first (added 2026-07-08):** Even once the user says "commit," show the drafted commit message in the chat turn first, then commit (in that same turn, no extra round-trip needed unless the user objects to the message). Why: user asked to see the message before it's used, so they can review/edit wording before it lands in history.

**Use `git commit -F <file>`, not inline `-m "$(cat <<'EOF' ...)"` (added 2026-07-10):** Draft the message, write it to a scratchpad file with the Write tool, show its contents in chat as the preview, then run `git commit -F <path>`. Why: passing the message inline via a heredoc broke repeatedly whenever the message contained an apostrophe (`picker's`, `it's`) — something outside my own command also wraps the whole shell invocation in single quotes (likely a logging/sandboxing layer doing `eval '<command>'`), and a literal apostrophe anywhere in the text prematurely closes that outer quoting since single quotes can't be escaped from within themselves. Writing the message to a file sidesteps shell quoting entirely — apostrophes, quotes, backticks are all safe in file content. `-F` also naturally satisfies the "show the message first" rule above, since the file is written (and can be shown) before the commit runs. This is purely a workaround for how *I* invoke shell commands in this sandboxed environment — not relevant to a human contributor or a rule about repo content — so it's memory, not CLAUDE.md.

**Skip `git status` / `git add`, pass pathspecs straight to `git commit` (added 2026-07-10):** Default commit command is now `git commit -F <message-file> -- <path1> <path2> ...`, listing exactly the files touched this turn. `git commit <pathspec>` stages and commits only those paths' current working-tree content, regardless of what else is dirty elsewhere — no preceding `git add` needed. `git status` is skippable too since I already know which files I edited from my own tool calls this session; I don't need to discover that via status. Why: user asked for a leaner commit flow after watching the status→add→commit dance every time. Caveat: this repo has had stray unrelated modified files show up before (e.g. `frontend/wailsjs/runtime/*` regenerated by a `wails dev` run outside the session) — always naming explicit paths on `git commit` is what keeps those out, so don't switch to `git commit -a` or `git add -A` even though they'd also skip the status/add dance.
